earlier_scan.source_named: Rumsey, Alan. 2000. Bunuba. In Dixon & Blake (eds.), Handbook of Australian Languages vol. 5, 35-153. OUP; also Knight 2004 Aspects of Bunuba grammar (UNE thesis). Neither reachable online.

new_statements.quote: The stress patterns on monomorphemic nominals and other word classes, such as mode particles, is straightforward and non-contrastive, and typical of other Australian languages. Words of between one and three syllables show primary stress on the first syllable. Words of four or five syllables show primary stress on the first syllable with secondary stress on the third syllable. Monomorphemic words of more than five syllables do not occur. [...] When case markers or enclitics are attached to a nominal the following stress patterns arise: if the case marker/enclitic is monosyllabic it receives no stress; if the ending is two or more syllables, it receives secondary stress on its first syllable.
new_statements.citation: Knight, Emily Jane. 2004. Aspects of Bunuba grammar and semantics. MA (Hons) thesis, University of New England, Armidale. Chapter 2, sec. 2.5 Stress, pp. 24-25.

The first quoted paragraph is there word for word: "The stress patterns on monomorphemic nominals and other word classes, such as mode particles, is straightforward and non-contrastive, and typical of other Australian languages. Words of between one and three syllables show primary stress on the first syllable. Words of four or five syllables show primary stress on the first syllable with secondary stress on the third syllable. Monomorphemic words of more than five syllables do not oc…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is fixed on the first syllable of the word (examples wíyi 'woman', bálga 'barramundi', gúmani 'knee', jálungùrru 'good', bályamàrada 'motorcar'); it is non-contrastive. Four- and five-syllable monomorphemic words add a secondary stress on the third syllable. Monosyllabic case markers and enclitics are unstressed; a case marker or enclitic of two or more syllables carries a secondary stress on its own first syllable (búga-yàni 'child-PL', míyha-bìlinyi 'meat-PERL', gúrama-yàni 'man-PL').
new_statements.secondary_stress: On the third syllable of 4-5 syllable monomorphemic words (jálungùrru, bályamàrada); on the first syllable of any polysyllabic case marker/enclitic (búga-yàni, míyha-bìlinyi); monosyllabic endings get none.
new_statements.exceptions: Fn. 2 (p. 58) suggests the long vowel in jarraa 'far away' might reflect stress with lengthening placed on the second syllable to emphasise distance iconically; wíyi 'woman' is listed as one phonetic syllable [wi:]. Stress in verbs (coverb + auxiliary complexes) is not described in sec. 2.5, which covers nominals, mode particles and other word classes; ch. 1 notes phonological evidence that coverb and auxiliary interact as a single word (sec. 3.3, chapter 3 file not among the open files).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level: monomorphemic nominals, mode particles and 'other word classes', and nominal plus case marker/enclitic; described impressionistically from fieldwork with ten Junjuwa (Fitzroy Crossing) speakers of both the light and heavy dialects; no instrumental data.
new_statements.identity_note: Knight 2004 describes contemporary Bunuba as spoken at Junjuwa (Fitzroy Crossing), with consultants from both the 'light' (western) and 'heavy' dialects (sec. 1.3.1, Table 1-3); the stress rule is given for the language as a whole with no dialect split. Same variety as Glottolog buna1275 (ISO bck).

sources.note: First-hand: stress is non-contrastive; words of 1-3 syllables have primary stress on the first syllable; words of 4-5 syllables have primary stress on the first and secondary on the third syllable; monomorphemic words of more than five syllables do not occur; a monosyllabic case marker/enclitic is unstressed, a 2+ syllable ending takes secondary stress on its first syllable (buga-yani, miyha-bilinyi, gurama-yani). Fn. 2 (p. 58): long vowel of jarraa 'far away' possibly stress shifted to 2nd syllable for iconic emphasis.
No stress line; cites Rumsey 2000 and Knight 2004/2008 for classification and dialects only.
